blocks.p: The Linnet sailed from Plenty at the turn of the watch with every pod in her hold spoken for, and Lyda Thorne sat on the edge of the last one in the row with her coat buttoned to the throat and made her own ship wait.

Nobody said anything. The loaders sat down on the bales. The master stood at the foot of the ramp with the manifest under his arm and looked at the refinery fires, and the deckhand sent to see to her seal stood off a little way, as if she were a hull that might still want something.

Four days from Earth. The church packet had brought her to Plenty under the Hierarch’s hand, and the wardens on it had been kind to her, the way people are kind to a foreigner who has had bad news in a language they do not speak. The case at her feet was Sol’s old travel case, packed in her nightgown on a rain night not quite a week ago, in another life. It had come back to her at the courts with a tag on the handle in a stranger’s hand, lighter by one shirt.

She had not brought the books. He had left them on the pier in Tobin’s lap, for Teo, and she had been glad of it at the courts, where they went through the case with gentle hands, and she was gladder now. What she had of his was his reading lenses, folded, and a pencil. She had put the lenses that morning in the inside pocket of her coat, over the place where she had laid her hand on his chest the last night and felt it warm, and buttoned the pocket. They would come up out of the cold with her, and not in the hold with the freight.
That was the whole of what she knew. She had put her hand on him and he had been warm.

The rest she had turned over for four days, like a figure that would not come right, and it still would not. She had held his right hand and counted, and felt something stop in him, and she did not know who she had been holding; she never had, not for certain, and she had married him anyway in front of forty people.
She would have to tell Tobin.

She had tried on the packet to find the words, and there were none. There would be no telling. She would go down the pier at the end of the day with the case in her hand, and the old man in the chair would reach out without looking and take hold of a wrist, and it would be hers. She would stand and let him hold it. Then she would give him the one thing she had carried home for him: that in that room, with everything he had ever wanted laid on the table, Sol had said a dockworker poured the water. She would tell him that and nothing else, and he would know the rest from the weight.
Teo she would tell what she had promised to.
The master came up the ramp with the manifest and did not hold it out, and she saw that he was waiting to be told whether the line was still a line.
“Bishop’s minute,” she said, and put out her hand for it.

Nobody laughed. She had not meant them to. Before she took the master’s pen she went to the crew’s basin at the foot of the ramp and set the hot tap running, and held her hand under it with the pen in it until the knuckles would close. She did not turn her back to do it. There was nobody left to hide it from.
She ran her eye down the figures, and they were right. Then she came to the line at the bottom, and her hand stopped above it by itself, and waited.
She had been signing for this line since she was nineteen and had never thought about it at all. She thought about it now. It took about as long as it had taken him.
It was reed. She signed, the gull lifting off the post, and gave the sheet back.
“Close me up,” she said. “The rest of them are cold.”

The deckhand checked the seal, and then, because somebody had taught him, checked it again. She let him. The lid came down. The frost came up the glass in its white ferns, and the hold went quiet, pod by pod.

She knew where it would come for her. Not here; this was her line, and she had never yet wept on it. It would be the counting-house stair, on the landing, halfway, where she had stood every morning for a year and let him breathe. She knew what it would cost her. She would pay it there.
Then the cold came in from the edges, and she went down into it like anyone.
